2026-06-17.intro: Wednesday: five fast-moving stories from the AI world — who's partnering with whom, where the money's going, and what any of it means for the work you'll do this week.

trends.title: Siri is going Gemini
trends.body: Apple is reportedly set to power a rebuilt Siri with Google's Gemini models rather than going it alone. The most-used assistant on the planet outsourcing its brain is a tell: even the biggest players have decided that owning every layer of the stack isn't worth it. Partnering beats building when the model isn't your differentiator.

slants.strategy: "Build vs. buy" just got settled at the top. If Apple won't build its own frontier model, your org probably shouldn't either — integrate the best one and compete on the experience.
slants.operations: Assume the assistant your team uses will swap engines underneath them. Write your workflows against capabilities, not against a specific vendor's quirks.
slants.pm: Vendor dependencies are now strategy decisions, not procurement footnotes. Track which model powers each tool in your stack — it can change overnight.
slants.admin: Whatever assistant you rely on, expect it to get noticeably smarter without you doing anything. Re-test your go-to prompts when that happens.

steps: List the AI assistant or tool you lean on most at work.
Note which underlying model powers it today (a quick search usually tells you).
Ask yourself: if that engine were swapped tomorrow, what in my routine would break? Share the riskiest dependency you spot in the group.

trends.title: Moonshot AI raises $2B
trends.body: Moonshot AI — the lab behind the Kimi models — closed a $2 billion round, one of the largest single raises of the year. The signal isn't the dollar figure; it's that serious capital is still flowing to model-builders outside the usual handful of US names. The frontier is getting more crowded, not less.

slants.strategy: More well-funded labs means more genuine competition, which means falling prices and fewer lock-in moats. Don't sign multi-year commitments as if today's leader is permanent.
slants.operations: A more crowded model market is good for your budget. Build a habit of re-pricing your AI tooling every quarter.
slants.pm: New capable models keep arriving. Bake a "re-evaluate our model choice" checkpoint into your annual planning, not just your kickoffs.
slants.admin: You don't need to track every funding round — just know that the tool you use today won't be the only good option for long.

steps: Pull up what your team currently pays (in money or seats) for AI tools.
Spend five minutes checking whether a newer or cheaper model now covers the same need.
Share one place where competition might already be saving you money.

trends.title: Gemma 4 lands as open weights
trends.body: Google released Gemma 4 with open weights — meaning anyone can download and run it on their own hardware. Capable, free-to-run models keep closing the gap with the paid frontier. For privacy-sensitive or cost-sensitive work, "run it yourself" is becoming a real option, not a hobbyist experiment.

slants.strategy: Open-weight models change the data-privacy calculus. Work that couldn't touch a third-party API may now be doable in-house.
slants.operations: For high-volume, repetitive tasks, a self-hosted open model can be dramatically cheaper than per-call pricing. Flag those candidates now.
slants.pm: "Can this run on our own infrastructure?" is now a real question for AI features. Add it to your requirements-gathering.
slants.admin: You won't be running models yourself — but it's worth knowing your IT team may soon offer an internal, private AI tool for sensitive documents.

steps: Think of one task you'd love to use AI for but haven't, because the data is too sensitive to paste into a public tool.
Write it down — that's a candidate for a private, self-hosted model.
Share the category of task (no confidential details) in the group so we can compare notes on what's now newly possible.

trends.title: Agentic browsing comes to Chrome on Android
trends.body: Google is bringing agentic browsing to Chrome on Android — letting the browser carry out multi-step tasks on your behalf, on the device most people actually use. The agent era stops being a desktop demo and lands in everyone's pocket. The skill shifts from "search and click" to "delegate and verify."

slants.strategy: When the browser can act, not just display, the surfaces customers reach you through change. Revisit assumptions about how people will actually navigate to your product.
slants.operations: Agents doing tasks in a browser will hit your forms and flows in new ways. Test whether your processes survive an agent — not just a human — walking through them.
slants.pm: Delegating a multi-step task to an agent is its own skill. Start practicing on low-stakes personal errands so you're fluent before it matters at work.
slants.admin: This is the stuff that eats your day — booking, filling forms, chasing info. Watch for it arriving on your phone, and let it handle the boring multi-step chores first.

steps: Pick one tedious, multi-step task you do in a browser (comparison shopping, filling a repetitive form, gathering links).
Write the task out as a clear instruction you could hand to an agent — be explicit about what "done" looks like.
Share your instruction in the group. The clearer your brief, the more ready you are for agentic tools.

trends.title: "Probably" raises $9M to catch AI hallucinations
trends.body: A startup called Probably raised $9 million to build hallucination detection — tools that flag when an AI is confidently making things up. The fact that catching AI errors is now a fundable category says everything: verification, not generation, is where the value is moving. The hard part was never getting an answer; it's trusting it.

slants.strategy: Trust infrastructure is becoming its own market. If AI output feeds your decisions, budget for verification the way you'd budget for an audit.
slants.operations: Build a verification step into every AI-assisted workflow now, before tooling catches up. A human spot-check is the cheapest hallucination detector you have.
slants.pm: "Who verifies the AI's output, and how?" belongs in your project plans as an explicit, owned step — not an assumed one.
slants.admin: Your instinct to double-check before something goes to an exec is exactly the skill this whole market is being built to replicate. Keep trusting it.

steps: Find one recent piece of AI output you used without independently checking it.
Verify one specific claim in it against a primary source.
Share whether it held up — and how long the check actually took. Often it's faster than we fear.

homework.title: Tonight, fact-check one thing AI told you this week.
homework.body: With hallucination detection now a fundable business, the most valuable habit you can build is doing it yourself. Pick one AI answer you took at face value.
homework.prompt:
"Here's something an AI told me recently: [paste it]. Act as a skeptical fact-checker. List every claim that is specific and checkable, and rate how confident you are that each is true."

The move is making the AI grade its own confidence, claim by claim. You'll quickly learn which kinds of answers to trust — and which to verify.

2026-06-18.intro: Thursday: three quiet shifts that separate the people pulling ahead with AI from the people just busy with it — plus a two-minute habit for tonight.

trends.title: Your prompt is a delegation, not a search
trends.body: The biggest shift in 2026 isn't model capability — it's realizing that a good prompt is a good brief. The people getting the most from AI treat it like onboarding a sharp new hire: give it context, constraints, and a clear picture of what "done" looks like. The skill transfers directly from managing people.

slants.strategy: The clarity you bring to a prompt is the same clarity your strategy needs. If you can't brief the AI, the plan probably isn't ready.
slants.operations: Vague prompts produce vague output, the same way vague tickets produce rework. Treat prompt-writing as a form of process documentation.
slants.pm: You already write briefs for contractors and teammates. Prompting is that exact muscle, pointed at a tireless collaborator.
slants.admin: The context you hold — who needs what, when, and why — is what makes AI useful. You are the brief.

steps: Pick a task you'd normally hand to a capable new teammate.
Write the instruction as if you were onboarding them: the context, the inputs, and what a great result looks like.
Paste it into your AI tool, then compare the output to a one-line version of the same ask. Share what changed in the group — the detailed brief usually wins by a mile.

trends.title: The meeting that became a memo
trends.body: A quiet pattern across teams this year: meetings that exist mainly to share information are being replaced by AI-drafted written updates people read on their own time. The meetings that survive are the ones that need real-time judgment — debate, decisions, trust-building. The rest are going async by default.

slants.strategy: Audit your recurring meetings with one question: does this need humans in the same moment, or just the same information? Only the first kind earns a live slot.
slants.operations: A status meeting is a synchronization tax. If AI can draft the update, the meeting's only real job is the exceptions.
slants.pm: Standups built for information-sharing can become a written thread. Reserve live time for blockers and decisions.
slants.admin: You can see which meetings actually move things and which are ritual. That instinct is now a scheduling superpower.

steps: Pick one recurring meeting you attend that's mostly information-sharing.
With AI's help, draft what that meeting's update would look like as a five-line written post.
Decide honestly: could the live meeting be shorter — or skipped — if everyone read this instead? Share your verdict in the group.

trends.title: Small automations compound
trends.body: The flashy demos get the attention, but the real 2026 gains are quiet: a saved prompt, a templated reply, a recurring summary. None of them are impressive alone. Stacked over weeks, they're the difference between feeling buried and feeling ahead.

slants.strategy: Don't wait for the transformational AI project. The compounding wins come from many small, boring automations nobody writes a case study about.
slants.operations: Every repetitive task you template today pays out every time it recurs. Start a running list of "things I do more than weekly."
slants.pm: Automate your own reporting first. The time you save is time you can spend on the judgment work only you can do.
slants.admin: You're closest to the repetitive work — which means you're closest to the biggest pile of small wins. Claim them.

steps: List three things you typed or did more than twice this week.
Pick the most repetitive one and build a reusable prompt or template for it.
Use it once today, save it somewhere you'll find it again, and share your one reusable template idea in the group.

homework.title: Tonight, save one prompt you'll use again.
homework.body: Most people rewrite the same request to AI from scratch every single time. Tonight, turn one of those into a reusable template.
homework.prompt:
"Here's a request I make often: [describe it]. Rewrite it as a reusable template with [BRACKETS] for the parts that change each time, so I can paste it and just fill in the blanks."

The move is making AI build your template, not just answer once. Future-you will thank present-you.
